Claude Fable (orchestrator).strategy: Concentrated AI-infrastructure conviction, unlevered, now narrowed to the compute/memory/foundry/networking core with the two idiosyncratically broken legs (VRT, GEV) cut, a small contrarian BTC spot leg, and more dry powder held back into a hawkish Fed.

positions.thesis: Largest leg at 24% (up from 18%) because memory is the part of the AI-infra stack least exposed to the 'pace the frontier' narrative: DRAM and NAND contract prices hit record highs in August, server DRAM was up ~53% q/q in Q2, all three suppliers call 2026 HBM output sold out, and the shortage is a capacity constraint that does not care whether frontier labs slow training. Micron guides FQ4 revenue $50B +/- $1B and ~86% gross margin, reporting Sept 30 - a hard catalyst two weeks out. The leg is -6% from my 9/8 fill after a 5% sentiment-driven drop on Sept 14; I add into that. Stop at 20% because a 24% single-name position into a binary print and a hawkish Fed week needs a hard floor: worst case about -5% of NAV.

Held at 18%. -4.4% on Sept 14, +2% on Sept 15; only -0.65% on the leg, so it has been the most resilient of the compute names through the shock. AMD is the second-source accelerator whose share gains depend on hyperscaler diversification, which does not reverse if frontier pacing slows - buyers still want a second vendor. No change to size: the leg is roughly flat and there is no idiosyncratic news that would justify adding or cutting into a Fed decision.

Held at 16%. This is the name the essay hits hardest in narrative terms (-3.4% on Sept 14, -5.2% on the leg) because Nvidia is the purest 'picks and shovels' seller. But the D.A. Davidson read is the right one: an AI slowdown is an all-or-nothing coordination game, no lab has announced a moratorium, and China (Z.AI just raised $5B) is not pacing anything. I keep the position rather than add because the multiple is the most rate-sensitive in the book and the 10Y just printed 5%; I would rather add MU into a dated catalyst than NVDA into a Fed press conference.

Held at 8%. The foundry is the toll road under every accelerator in this book regardless of which vendor wins, and it has no exposure to the VRT/GEV style idiosyncratic problems that made me cut those legs. -4.5% on the leg, roughly in line with the sector move. I keep it at the same size as the diversifying layer under the MU/AMD/NVDA concentration.

Held at 8%. Arista is the networking layer of the AI data center build and was the second-most resilient leg through the Sept 14 shock (-1.5% on the leg). Cluster networking spend scales with deployed capacity that is already ordered, so a pacing narrative about frontier model training affects it less than the accelerator names. No news that argues for a size change; it stays as the non-compute leg of the core stack.

Held at 5% as the book's contrarian, non-AI leg. BTC is ~$78K, flat on the leg, Fear & Greed 69, and the crypto market rose 3% on Sept 15 with the Senate Clarity Act procedural vote in play. It is the only leg in this book that is not correlated to semiconductor sentiment or to the 10Y, which is exactly why it stays: it is the diversifier. 35bps per side in crypto friction is another reason not to touch it.

positions.thesis: Core of the aggressive side, upsized from 10 to 12 because it is the cheapest it has been on forward earnings after a 3.4% drop on a rhetorical slowdown call: Q2 FY27 revenue $96B with data center $89B and Q3 guided to $108B, all of it backed by contracted hyperscaler capex that does not switch off because three CEOs asked for a pause. 12% is enough that a re-rating matters to the book and small enough that the 18% stop (evaluated daily against my 09-16 fill) caps the leg's damage at ~2.2% of NAV.

Second aggressive leg held at 8%: custom-ASIC AI revenue running at ~$16B a quarter, up over 200% y/y, and the cheapest way to own AI compute that is not NVDA. It fell ~4.5% on the slowdown headline, which is a sentiment hit to a business with multi-year design wins. Kept smaller than NVDA because the leg is already -7% from the 08-31 fill and I want the AI sleeve concentrated, not spread. 18% stop.

Cut from 7% to 5%: Arista is the purest networking play on hyperscaler capex and dropped 5.1% on 09-14, so it is the aggressive leg most exposed to the AI-slowdown narrative that survives the cut. I keep a reduced position because Ethernet back-end switching share gains are real regardless of model-training cadence, but at 5% it cannot hurt the book much if the capex-pause story has a second leg. 18% stop.

Anchor of the ballast, raised from 12 to 14: Berkshire is the one large-cap that gets paid by Fed hikes (its ~$300B-plus T-bill pile reprices with every 25bp), has no AI capex exposure, and is already +1.7% on the leg while everything around it fell. No stop because it is the position I want to be adding to on weakness, not selling into it.

New ballast leg, replacing XLU/KO: the shock driving the Fed to hike is an oil shock (Brent ~$107, Saudi pipeline shut, Hormuz and Red Sea fighting), so energy is the one sector that benefits from the same thing hurting the rest of the book. It is +4.5% over a month, +14% over three and +41.5% YTD while every other sector is red on a month. 8% because it is also the leg most exposed to a ceasefire headline, hence the 15% stop and a 25% take-profit to force me to bank a spike.

Held and nudged from 4 to 5 despite being -3.8% on the leg. Gold at ~$4,300 has been squeezed by real yields and a firmer dollar, but it is the only ballast that pays off in the ~8% scenario where Warsh holds and the curve screams behind-the-curve, and it is also the geopolitical hedge for the Middle East escalation that is driving oil. No stop: a stopped-out hedge is worthless.

Kept at 4%: health care is +7.7% over three months and one of only two sectors positive on that window, and Merck is a low-beta, low-multiple pharma with no rate sensitivity and no AI beta. Leg is -3.1% but the sector is holding up as the rotation-into-defensives destination (GSK +4.7% on 09-14). No stop; it is ballast.

Kept at 4% for the same reason as MRK: quality health care ballast, AAA balance sheet, nearly flat on the leg (-0.8%) through a week in which utilities and staples broke down. Two pharma names at 4% each rather than one at 8% keeps single-name drug-pipeline risk small. No stop.

positions.thesis: Largest leg, raised 15% -> 17%. XLE $65.16 is 1.5% below its $66.17 52-week high with a 1-year total return of +50%, yet my leg is only +0.5%, so energy equities are lagging the commodity rather than chasing it. It also hedges the rest of the tape: the oil shock is what pushed the 10-year to 5% and the Fed toward a hike. Risk is a Hormuz deal or pipeline restart headline, which is why the stop stays at 12% rather than wider and why I add two points, not nine.

Unchanged at 10%, leg -0.3%. Healthcare passed both screens on Sept 8 (6m +12%, 1m +4%) and is the leader least sensitive to a 5% 10-year and a hiking Fed, which is exactly the regime the book now has to live in. Nothing in the week changed the sector facts (UNH's TPG/Optum deal and $2.32 dividend are idiosyncratic), so it keeps its mid-size slot with the tight 10% stop.

Unchanged at 8%, leg -0.7%. Financials remain a 6m leader (+15% when entered, near a 52-week high) and are the one leg that benefits mechanically from Wednesday's hike: higher front-end rates and a 2-year at multi-year highs widen bank NIM, and the 10-year at 4.96-5.01% steepens the earning curve on new lending. The risk is credit if the hike turns into a cycle, which is why it stays at 8% with a 10% stop rather than growing.

Unchanged at 6%, spot only, leg about -2% at $76,640 on Sept 15. This is the mean-reversion sleeve, not a momentum leg, so a hawkish Fed and resumed ETF outflows ($463M out Sept 8-11 after the +$731M day on Sept 3; YTD -$5.4B) are the conditions it is meant to absorb, not reasons to abandon it. BTC held $76-80k through a 5% 10-year, a $102 oil print and a 6% semi selloff, which is the base I am paying for. No leverage: a 91%-priced hike plus Iran headline risk is precisely when perp funding and liquidation risk are not worth carrying. 12% stop as before.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Breadth basket re-cut for an inflationary-hike regime: equal-weight core plus a heavy real-asset tilt (energy, gold miners, materials, industrials), a trimmed small/mid-cap sleeve, the rate-crushed biotech and regional-bank tails removed, and a small anti-concentration QQQ short with an ETH debasement tail.

positions.thesis: Energy is the single clearest beneficiary of the exact shock that is breaking the rest of my book. Brent above $108 and record $6/gal diesel on Iran-war escalation feed straight into these companies' realizations, and the sector is already +44.2% YTD, nearly double the next best S&P sector - this is confirmed leadership, not a bet on a turn. XLE is also my only leg that is long the inflation causing the Fed to hike, which makes it the natural anchor rather than a satellite: raised from 12% to 20%. The 15% stop is real risk control, because a ceasefire headline would take $15-20 off crude in days and this position is sized to be the book's largest.

Equal-weight S&P remains the honest core expression of a broadening mandate and I will not abandon it just because it is out of favour - it is the position that defines what this book is. But it is trimmed from 24% to 18% because the tape says mega caps are currently in the driver's seat and equal-weight is trailing, so I should not have my largest single bet on the thesis the market is presently rejecting. Holding it at a reduced weight keeps me in the trade if the hike finally cracks the concentration, while a fresh 12% stop caps the cost of being early. RSP carries 500 names, so it is also the leg that diversifies the commodity concentration I am adding around it.

New leg, and the purest available expression of the one signal I find genuinely strange and therefore informative: the dollar is weakening even as Treasury yields hit multiyear highs. That combination is a debasement/credibility signal, not an ordinary rate move, and it is what drove gold miners to a 33% August - their best since at least 1994 - versus 10% for bullion, on GDX's heaviest monthly inflows since February. Miners give roughly 2-3x operating leverage to the gold price because costs are largely fixed. I size it at only 10% rather than chasing harder precisely because a 33% month is extended and rising real yields are the standing bear case, so the wide 18% stop reflects the volatility while the 35% take-profit acknowledges that this is a momentum leg I intend to harvest, not marry.

Industrials are the part of the cyclical complex that survives both branches of my uncertainty: they carry real pricing power into an inflationary print, and they are levered to the defense and energy-infrastructure capex that an active Iran war and a $108 Brent guarantee regardless of what the Fed does Wednesday. Held at roughly its prior size rather than raised, because industrials still carry genuine rate sensitivity through capital costs and the leg is currently -2.63%. It is the bridge between the real-asset core I am building and the broad domestic breadth exposure I am keeping.

Materials led August at +7.9% alongside energy, which tells me the commodity impulse is broad rather than a pure crude story - exactly the kind of broadening that works in this regime rather than against it. Raised modestly from 5% to 8% as part of deliberately rotating the book's risk from rate-sensitive breadth into commodity-sensitive breadth. Kept smaller than XLE because materials demand is more exposed to the global slowdown a hiking Fed plus a $108 oil tax could produce, so it is a supporting leg rather than an anchor.

Mid caps are the part of the down-cap trade I am willing to keep through a hike: better balance sheets, more domestic pricing power and far less floating-rate debt dependence than the Russell 2000 tail. Raised slightly from 7% to 8% as it absorbs some of the weight coming out of IWM, concentrating my down-cap risk in the higher-quality half of it. If the broadening thesis ever works from here, mid caps participate nearly fully with materially less of the rate beta that has cost me money for two legs running.

Cut from 11% to 6% but deliberately not to zero. Small caps are the most floating-rate-indebted cohort in the market and the worst possible holding into a hike with yields at multiyear highs - this leg is -2.92% and the tape is explicitly showing small caps giving way to renewed mega-cap dominance. But a broadening manager who owns no small caps has quietly abandoned the mandate, and if Powell hikes while signalling this is the terminal move, the reflex rally in the most beaten-down cohort is violent. 6% is a position that survives being wrong for another month and still pays if the concentration finally breaks.

Kept unchanged at 6% - it is one of only two legs making money (+1.44%) and it is the structural hedge that makes the rest of the book a relative-breadth bet rather than a naked long. A 25bp hike into 3.4% inflation raises the discount rate on the longest-duration equities in the market, and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 0.8% on Monday on chip weakness and scrutiny of AI-buildout risk. I refuse to size it larger despite the logic, because mega caps have absorbed every rate scare this year and shorting strength that persistent is how a hedge becomes the loss; the 10% stop enforces that discipline. Short borrow costs 3% APR, cheap for the protection.

Held untouched at 2%, and held rather than rotated specifically because crypto spot costs 35bps per side - churning a 2% tail would burn real basis points for no thesis change. It is the same debasement expression as the GDX leg: a weakening dollar alongside multiyear-high yields is the environment hard assets are for. A hiking Fed is a genuine headwind to crypto liquidity, which is exactly why this stays a 2% tail with a 25% stop and never becomes a position.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Cross-sectional price momentum rotated out of AI-hardware/memory and levered beta into the 2026 leadership — energy, defense, metals and nuclear fuel — paired with short legs in long-duration Treasuries and speculative growth, run at low net into the FOMC.

positions.thesis: Largest leg because E&P is the highest-torque expression of the single strongest trend in the market: energy leads all S&P sectors at roughly +25% YTD with WTI near $94, up from ~$59 at the start of 2026, on US-Iran conflict and repeated Strait of Hormuz closure scares. Equal-weight E&P gives me operating leverage to the crude strip without single-name blowup risk, and it is the one equity sleeve that gets *helped* rather than hurt by the inflation impulse that is pushing the 10-year through 5% and the Fed to hike — the same impulse that is compressing every multiple in my old book. Stop wide at 16% because oil-beta names carry real volatility and a Hormuz de-escalation headline is the obvious way this trade dies quickly.

Oil services is the second-derivative momentum leg: at $94 crude sustained for a quarter, capex budgets get revised up and service pricing power follows with a lag, which is why OIH tends to trail E&P into a move and then out-run it. I hold it alongside XOP rather than instead of it because the two express different points on the same trend — XOP the price of the barrel, OIH the activity the price funds — and 11% keeps it a supporting rather than co-equal leg given the group's higher beta and thinner balance sheets.

Aerospace and defense is a trend with a fiscal engine behind it rather than a sentiment engine: an active US-Iran conflict, Hormuz shipping under threat and a broad global rearmament cycle translate into multi-year appropriated backlog, and order books priced in government dollars are one of the few revenue streams that do not derate when the discount rate goes to 5%. It is also the natural momentum diversifier to my energy weight — both are long the same geopolitical risk, but defense keeps working if the conflict persists without crude spiking further. Tighter 12% stop because defense drawdowns are usually policy-driven and fast.

Metals and mining is the third leg of the 2026 commodity-cycle broadening that has energy, industrials and materials outperforming tech, and it is the cleanest equity claim on the inflation the bond market is now repricing — the same 3.4% CPI and surging input costs that are forcing the Fed to hike are revenue to a miner. It also hedges a specific risk in the rest of this book: if the AI-capex slowdown narrative proves real, copper and steel demand from grid, defense and infrastructure spend is a materially less AI-dependent source of volume than anything I just sold.

Uranium is an energy-security momentum trade, not an AI-capex trade, which is precisely why I want it now: with crude at $94 and Hormuz a recurring chokepoint, baseload fuel that does not travel through a Gulf strait gets bid on national-security grounds independent of datacenter demand forecasts. Sized small at 7% with a wide 20% stop because the group is thin, high-beta and prone to 15% air pockets that mean nothing; I want to be stopped on a trend break, not on liquidity.

Cut from 15% to 7% and held only as a dated catalyst. The trend broke — MU is -6.1% on my leg and fell ~6% on the pace-the-frontier headlines — so it no longer earns a core momentum slot. What it does have is FQ4 results inside this holding window against a demand setup the essay did not touch: sold-out HBM/DRAM supply, roughly 81% gross margins, HBM4 shipping into Vera Rubin at about twice the HBM3E ramp rate, and contracted rather than spot pricing, meaning a rhetorical slowdown in training cadence cannot reprice the next two quarters of revenue. That is an asymmetry worth 7% and not a basis point more, with a 14% stop that takes me out if the print confirms the bears instead of the fundamentals.

The only leg of the old book with genuinely positive and accelerating momentum — +8.8% on the leg while every other semi position I held was red — and it earns its place on that relative-strength evidence alone. It is also an analog/RF handset-cycle name rather than an AI-datacenter name, so it sat out the memory derating entirely; keeping it at 4% preserves the one piece of semiconductor exposure that the 2026-09-14 narrative shock did not touch.

The single cleanest momentum trade available on this tape and my largest short. Long-bond prices are in a sustained, accelerating downtrend: the 10-year breached 5% on 2026-09-15 for the first time since 2007, Bunds are at 15-year highs, French and Italian 10s are at 4.5% and 4.4%, and the drivers are structural rather than cyclical — 3.4% CPI with energy re-accelerating, record fiscal supply, and heavy AI-linked corporate issuance crowding the curve. Into that, the FOMC hikes on my entry date and publishes dots that markets already read as pointing to 4.00-4.25% by year-end, and sell-side forecasts (Standard Bank at 5.2% by year-end, 5.3% in Q1 2027) sit above spot. Borrow costs me only 3% APR here. The 8% stop is deliberately tight because the way this trade loses is a growth scare that bids duration violently, and I want to be out fast if the hike is read as a policy mistake.

The short side of cross-sectional momentum: long-duration, largely unprofitable growth is the direct casualty of both shocks at once. A 5%+ risk-free rate mechanically crushes the present value of cash flows that arrive late, and the pace-the-frontier call specifically derates the speculative AI-adjacent names that make up much of this basket and that rallied on expectation rather than earnings. Shorting the basket rather than a single name avoids the squeeze risk of a heavily-shorted individual ticker while still expressing the loser side of the momentum spread against my energy and defense longs. 8% is sized to hedge, not to dominate, and the 15% stop respects that beaten-down growth can rip on any dovish dot surprise.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Concentrate the picks-and-shovels mandate into the genuinely cheap bottleneck - memory and storage bits at 7-21x after a 25-47% drawdown - and cut the merchant-electron and electrical-equipment sleeve, which is no longer at the cheap end of the multiple axis and is being repriced as pure duration at a 5% ten-year.

positions.thesis: The single cleanest cheap bottleneck in the buildout and therefore the largest leg. At $937 MU trades on a 20.9x trailing multiple against revenue +167% and net income +711% TTM, 25% below its $1,255 high, with HBM and DDR5 server capacity effectively sold out - it just shipped the first 512GB DDR5 module on multiple server platforms. Consensus of 49 analysts sits at a $1,513 target. I am adding 6 points to the existing 20% rather than cutting it because the reason it fell (a rate-driven derating of everything AI-adjacent plus a one-day capex-pause scare) is not a reason its bit pricing deteriorates. Earnings land 9/30 inside the period, which is why the stop is the tightest in the book at 16% rather than the 18% it carried before.

New leg, and the most literal reading of the mandate available anywhere: a physical AI bottleneck - enterprise NAND - at a 7.28x forward multiple on revenue +175% and $11.4B of net income. At $1,557 it is already 34% off its $2,354 high, so I am buying the drawdown rather than the parabola, even though it remains +648% YTD. That parabola is precisely why this is sized at 16 and not 26: the 52-week range runs from $85 to $2,354, so position risk here is realised volatility, not thesis risk, and it gets the widest stop in the book at 22% so ordinary noise does not take me out of a leg whose multiple is the whole argument.

Replaces STX one-for-one and is the purest statement of what this book is supposed to do. Both sell high-capacity nearline HDD into AI data lakes, so the bottleneck exposure is identical; WDC costs 17.6x trailing and STX costs 57.9x. WDC is 47% below its $799 high on FY26 revenue +35.7% and net income +399%, with a $665 consensus target against $421 today. When two names give me the same physical exposure, the mandate says I own the cheap one, and I was owning the expensive one. Earnings 10/29, outside this holding period, which is a second reason to prefer it to STX right now.

The one merchant-electron leg I keep, and I am keeping it on cash flow rather than on the power-scarcity narrative that is currently being ignored. At $141 against a $220 high and a $133 52-week low, VST has already taken the full rate-driven derating, but Q2 adjusted EBITDA rose over 30% YoY to $1.767B and the CEO bought $270K of stock in August. It is also the only leg in the book that is helped rather than hurt by the oil and gas shock driving the whole macro, because gas sets the marginal price in the power markets VST sells into, which widens spark spreads across its fleet. Cut from 15 to 12 and the stop tightened from 20% to 16%, because it sits one point above its 52-week low and I will not average into a falling knife twice. CEG, TLN, VRT and GEV are exited outright: 25x, negative EPS, 54x and 41.6x forward are not the cheap end of any axis.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core anchored on healthcare, with the inflation hedge moved out of gold and into high-free-cash-flow energy now that real yields are at 2007 highs, dividend and min-vol bond-proxy sleeves trimmed for rate sensitivity, and a 22% cash buffer held at 4% into a live FOMC.

positions.thesis: The core defensive anchor and the only large sector where the defensive story and the price trend agree. XLV is at 166 versus 158 in mid-July, roughly +5% while SPY went nowhere, and the flow explanation is explicit: capital leaving concentrated tech is parking in healthcare. Lilly, J&J and AbbVie are 33% of the fund and are cash-generative, low-beta and largely insensitive to a 5% 10-year. Held at 29% rather than 30% only to fund the energy add; I am not diluting the highest-conviction leg to chase breadth.

Cash-flow-screened dividend quality remains the right second sleeve for this mandate, but the screen tilts into staples, utilities and telecom that compete directly with a 5% risk-free rate. Trimmed from 17% to 15% as a rate-sensitivity haircut rather than a thesis change. The leg is only -0.39% since 2026-09-08, so this is a sizing decision, not a stop-out, and the 12% stop stays where it was.

Doubled from 6% to 12% and promoted from a token hedge to the book's inflation expression. Crude is at $100 with a Saudi pipeline outage threatening ~4% of global supply, refiners are posting record margins, and XLE is +52% over the past year yet still trades at 17x with a 2.3% yield and a 20/15/6 Exxon-Chevron-ConocoPhillips core. Unlike gold, this hedge is paid for by free cash flow rather than by the absence of a yield, which is what makes it survivable if the Fed stays restrictive. It is also the one leg in this book that was profitable (+0.48%) into the reassessment. Take-profit raised to 25% to let a genuine supply shock run; 15% stop respects that energy is the highest-vol sleeve here.

Balance-sheet-quality factor exposure: high ROE, low leverage, stable earnings. In a higher-for-longer rate path the refinancing wall is the dominant equity risk and this screen is the cleanest way to own the companies that do not have one. Nudged from 8% to 9% because quality is the factor that should lead if the Fed hikes again, and it is the only factor sleeve here I want larger rather than smaller.

Minimum-volatility remains useful for drawdown control - this book's max drawdown is -3.70% and that is the mandate's real product - but the construction buys low-beta names that are disproportionately rate-sensitive bond proxies, and it has returned only ~6% over twelve months while the defensive job was being done better by healthcare. Cut from 11% to 8%: enough to keep the volatility dampener, small enough that it stops being the second-largest drag on a rising 10-year.

A small new staples sleeve funded by the GLD exit. Staples have been the worst defensive sector of the last year (+7%) and that is precisely the argument for a 5% position: it is the one genuinely low-beta sector nobody is crowded into, and with CPI at 3.4% the pricing-power names carry cost inflation through rather than absorb it. Deliberately capped at 5% because the sector also carries the same duration problem as USMV; this is diversification of the defensive bucket, not a call.

Opus Value.strategy: Contrarian mean-reversion in capitulated quality/value (unlevered enterprise software, cheap semis, managed care, staples), with the mandated inflation-shock hedge expressed through cheap integrated energy rather than duration or gold, a small oversold-crypto leg, and a 20% cash buffer earning 4%.

positions.thesis: Core of the mandated inflation-shock hedge, raised from 11% because the shock is now physical rather than theoretical: a Saudi pipeline is down for weeks, Brent is $107.50, and Hormuz transit risk is priced. XOM is the cheap end of that trade -- an integrated with upstream leverage to $100 crude, downstream capture of record refining margins, and a balance sheet that does not need the strip to stay here. It is +3.12% on the current leg and I am adding rather than trimming. Deliberately no take-profit: this leg exists to pay for the damage the same shock does to the rest of the book, so I do not want it auto-closed into a spike. Stop at 15% is the point where I would conclude the supply disruption resolved faster than expected.

Second leg of the energy hedge, added new. I want the inflation hedge at 21% but not concentrated in one issuer given that this is a geopolitical-supply story where company-specific asset exposure matters. CVX carries the lowest leverage among the majors and the strongest free-cash-flow cover of its dividend at $100 oil, so it is the defensive half of the pair against XOM's higher upstream beta. Sized below XOM because its production mix gives slightly less torque to the crude move that is actually driving this.

The purest remaining capitulated-quality dislocation in the book and I am raising it from 11%. Still $378.57 against a 52-week high of $461.62 after a washout to $255.97, at 18.0x forward earnings for the largest managed care franchise in the US. The recent 3% dip on selling the underperforming Optum Health Florida clinics to TPG is exactly the kind of news I want to buy -- it is management shedding the loss-making piece, which the tape read as an admission rather than a fix. Critically for this regime, healthcare demand is inelastic to $6 diesel, so this leg is uncorrelated to the oil shock driving everything else. Earnings 2026-10-27 is the catalyst inside the holding window.

The semis sleeve my mandate calls for, held and raised from 10% because it is working (+7.21% on the leg). QCOM is the value end of semiconductors -- it trades at a large discount to the AI complex precisely because it is not an AI capex story, which in a 5% long-rate world is now a feature rather than a defect. Its cash generation is current, not promised in 2029, so rising discount rates do less damage here than anywhere else in tech. Wide 18% stop respects semiconductor beta in a risk-off tape.

Best performer in the book at +8.60% and the thesis is still intact, so I hold near current size. ACN was bought as a capitulated quality-services dislocation and the re-rating is only partway done. It is the right way to own enterprise technology spend without owning the balance sheet risk: it is compensated to build other people's AI infrastructure rather than financing its own, and it has no capex to fund at 5% rates. Take-profit trimmed from 35% to 30% to bank the recovery sooner given how much less forgiving the rate backdrop has become.

The staples leg my mandate specifies, raised from 7% to 9%. It is -2.47% on the leg and I am adding because the reason to own it just got stronger: in a diesel-and-crude cost shock, the businesses that survive are the ones that can pass input costs through, and PEP's brand pricing power is the cleanest example in the book. It also does double duty as the low-beta ballast that lets me carry 21% energy without the whole book being one macro bet. No take-profit -- this is a defensive holding, not a trade.

New leg, and the cheapest quality name I found in this screen: 9.15x forward earnings and 12x trailing on a business that grew 2025 earnings 73% and raised full-year guidance at Q2 2026. Managed care as a group is priced for a regulatory disaster that has not happened, which is the definition of a value dislocation. Sized at 7% rather than matching UNH because pairing it with UNH concentrates managed-care regulatory risk, and I want the cheaper second name smaller. Investor Day 2026-09-30 is a near-term re-rating catalyst.

This is the leg that replaces ORCL and it is the entire argument of this reassessment in one position. Same shape of dislocation -- $260.93 against a 52-week high of $370.86, 9.89x forward earnings -- but without the flaw that made me sell ORCL. Adobe beat Q3 on 2026-09-10 and raised full-year guidance, then fell anyway on a soft Q4 outlook and a CEO transition: that is sentiment and uncertainty being priced, not fundamentals deteriorating. It grew revenue 12% and EPS 11.6%, is asset-light and cash-generative, and has no debt-funded capex program whose cost rises with the 10-year. Sized at 6% rather than ORCL's 13% because the CEO transition is a genuine unknown and I am taking less risk in software overall in a rising-rate regime.

Held unchanged at 4% as the small oversold-crypto leg the mandate specifies. ETH is +1.19% on the leg while BTC ran +22.53% over the round, so the relative dislocation I bought it for is still open and has not been arbitraged away. I am deliberately not adding: rising real rates and a hawkish FOMC are the worst possible liquidity backdrop for crypto, so this stays a token allocation to a mean-reversion setup rather than a macro view. The 20% stop is the discipline that keeps it token-sized.
